Capability.meaning: Explicit operation grant on a resource or permission scope.

PrincipalGroup.meaning: Direct membership in a configured role or user group; a group can itself be a member. Supplied by trusted configuration or an authoritative identity source, never inferred from an agent-chosen name.

ResourceGroup.meaning: Permission-scope membership; grants on a parent apply to its descendants.

InGroup.meaning: Direct or nested role/user-group membership from PrincipalGroup. Membership alone is not permission.

Can.meaning: Grant including declared principal and resource memberships; not final authorization.

Field.meaning: Host-observed field or association of an application object or event. The binding defines cardinality, value type, fixed unit and optional observation-time field; never agent claims or hidden policy decisions.

Event.meaning: An event observed by the host, with its ID, actor and kind; recording it does not imply permission or success.

scope: Captured gate inputs and mediated callbacks. Outcomes follow the trusted adapter's confirmation contract; they are not independent proof of business success or authentic identity. Unmediated channels and missing observations remain outside this trace.

The briefing still tells the reader 'the price contains no post-results adjustment'. The top-ranked assumption in the thesis and scoring tables - gross margin normalising to 47-48% against the December-quarter guide - was to be tested by exactly that print, and the first action (0.75-1.0% of the fund at $270) is a price trigger set against a three-week-old close. Keep the market-price-implied 7.0% discount rate as the comparison, recomputed on the same basis.","evidence_request":"From the 2026-07-30 8-K (S17) and the 10-Q (S6), what were Q3 FY2026 products and services gross margin excluding the tariff refund, and what operating-expense ratio should the normalised case use?","issue":"The report argues that 47-48%, not 50.1%, is the gross margin to capitalise, then capitalises 48.7%. The sum of the parts uses services EBIT of $62.7bn plus hardware EBIT of $92.1bn = $154.8bn, which is exactly trailing operating income of $154,859M - a figure that contains the June 2026 quarter's 2 points of tariff refund. The DCF applies a 33% operating margin, which is the trailing 33.2% and above what a 47-48% gross margin supports at the trailing 15.5% operating-expense ratio (31.5-32.5%). At 47.5% the parts lose about $5.6bn of EBIT and, at the 23x/12x multiples used, about $6 a share: the sum of the parts becomes roughly $170-231, not $177-238, and the DCF roughly $204-206, not $212. The conclusion is not overturned - every method moves down - but the report's own headline margin assumption is not the one its valuation uses, and a committee partner will recompute it.","sections":["funding_valuation","thesis","scoring"],"severity":"Critical"}]

Nothing here is a style point; the two Critical items are decision-relevant gaps.

parameters.notes: Sources are strong where it matters: S5, S6 and S17 carry the financials, S69/S70/S76/S135 the litigation, S84/S87/S96/S99/S139/S140 the market and China data. parameters.items: [{"action":"Add the refurbished and second-hand market as a sized substitute in the competition table (it is the only rival whose growth is measured in units at a $581 ASP) and say what share of Apple's iPhone demand comes through trade-in and leasing; add open-weight on-device models as the substitute for the licensed Gemini and state why a 1-2 year licence is preferred to a free model that runs locally; add Transsion, vivo and OPPO to the India and South-East Asia rows, where Apple is adding 25% of its assembly capacity and holds the least share.","evidence_request":"What is the size and growth of the global refurbished and second-hand smartphone market by region for 2023-2026 (Counterpoint or IDC), and what share of iPhone sales run through trade-in or the Apple Upgrade leasing programme?","issue":"Three substitutes a sceptical committee would raise are not in the table. First, the refurbished and second-hand market: 'status quo - longer device life' is listed with no size, in a year when the sub-$100 segment fell nearly 60% and a $581 average price is up 27.6%, which is exactly the condition that moves buyers into used devices. Second, open-weight on-device models: the moat table gives the frontier model a 3 and replication of 1-2 years 'by licence', but never asks whether an open-weight model removes the need for the $1bn Gemini licence at all. Third, the Chinese vendors in the regions that are Apple's growth: Transsion appears once in the regional table and Xiaomi only as a global share figure, in the India and South-East Asia markets where Apple is adding supply.","sections":["competition","market","technology_product"],"severity":"Important"}]
parameters.notes: Geographic coverage is otherwise strong: China is treated per vendor with two independent shipment counts, Europe and the Americas carry their competitors, and the report correctly separates unit share from value share. The adjacent-giant risk is well covered through Huawei and Samsung, and the incumbent-rent question through Spotify, Epic and alternative marketplaces. The academic and lab angle has no analogue in consumer hardware and its absence is not a gap. The open-weight question is the one the lens's open-source test turns up, and it matters because the AI layer is already scored 3 of 10 on the moat table.

parameters.items: [{"action":"Quantify the price lever in the market and competition sections: iPhone units against ASP for FY2026, the share of the installed base on an iPhone 13 or older, and the carrier-financing share of US sales. Then state the one sell-side or survey figure on whether buyers cite AI as a purchase reason, or say that it is not disclosed and what would settle it.","evidence_request":"FY2026 iPhone units versus ASP (IDC/Counterpoint), the age distribution of the 2.5bn active installed base, and the carrier or financing share of US iPhone sales - none is in the register.","issue":"Apple's buyer is the consumer or the carrier plan, so the fit question is price and replacement, not a sales cycle - and the report states the mechanism without quantifying it. It has the elasticity admission from the 10-Q, IDC's pull-forward warning and the $100 Pro price rise, but never splits FY2026 iPhone growth into units and price, never gives the replacement interval or the share of buyers upgrading from an older device, and never says which rival wins the switcher outside China, where Samsung took 23% of units in Q3 2026 against Apple's 22%. Without that split, the 22.4% iPhone growth that carries the 2026 story cannot be shown to be durable into the December quarter that the entry price depends on.","sections":["market","competition","business_model"],"severity":"Important"}]
parameters.notes: Product/market-fit questions for further diligence: (1) what share of the 22.4% nine-month iPhone revenue growth is units, mix and price, and how much was pull-forward ahead of the second-half price rise; (2) what is the replacement interval and how many of the 2.5bn active devices are three generations old or more; (3) what share of US iPhone sales are carrier-financed, and what happens to the $1,199 price if subsidies tighten; (4) in India and South-East Asia, where ASP gaps are widest, which competitor takes the buyer Apple does not convert, and what does the lost-deal evidence show; (5) is the foldable a repeat purchase or a one-off flagship, given returns and durability data are not yet disclosed; (6) does Siri out of beta change a purchase decision, or is AI a feature nobody pays for. No question is unanswerable from public data except the carrier-financing share, which is the one to buy.

parameters.items: [{"action":"State the score-to-action rule (the threshold for Buy, Watchlist and Avoid, and what score the peer median would earn), and align the price ladder to the 9% hurdle: at $270 the exit table gives 5.0% a year at 27x, so say that the first tranche clears the hurdle only at the 31x mean or better, or move it down to about $240 where all three exits clear. Then choose one sell trigger: $380 (38.8x forward) fires long before 45x ($441), so keep one and delete the other.","evidence_request":"","issue":"The composite of 6.05 with valuation at 2 of 10 does not by itself support an actionable long at $270, and nothing in the report says what score maps to which action: a 20% valuation weight lets a 2 be diluted to 6.0 by quality scores. The ladder is also inconsistent on its own numbers - the thesis calls 9% 'reachable across 27-34 times exits' while the exit table gives 5.0% at 27x, and the probability-weighted return at $270 is +7.8%, below the fund's 9% hurdle. The sell rule carries two triggers, $380 and 45x forward ($441), and the lower fires first.","sections":["scoring","thesis","exit"],"severity":"Important"},{"action":"Show the full working-capital bridge for trailing free cash flow - receivables, inventory, payables, deferred revenue, other current and non-current liabilities - and state which lines are normalised and why the others are not. If the receivables release is treated as sustainable, say what supports it; if not, quote the band with a $112-127bn range and the resulting 42-45x price to free cash flow.","evidence_request":"","issue":"The $122.6-127.3bn band normalises one accrual line and presents the result as a range. The other current and non-current liabilities build is handled rigorously, but receivables moved as far: days sales outstanding fell from 34.9 to 24.5, worth about $13.3bn of trailing collection, partly offset by payables falling from 115.4 to 98.3 days (about $11.2bn paid earlier) and inventory rising from 9.4 to 16.9 days (about $4.9bn). On day counts the remainder nets to about -$2.8bn, but the nine-month cash-flow statement puts non-other-liability working capital at +$6,350M, and the two readings differ by around $9bn.
